newsitem.title: UK: SOCCER-NEWCASTLE HOPING DALGLISH WILL OUTSHINE KEEGAN AGAIN.
newsitem.headline: SOCCER-NEWCASTLE HOPING DALGLISH WILL OUTSHINE KEEGAN AGAIN.

text.p: Kenny Dalglish returned to the spotlight on Tuesday when he was named as Kevin Keegan's successor as the manager of Newcastle United.

The 45-year-old former Celtic and Liverpool player who has won virtually every major honour in the game as a both player and manager, was welcomed to Newcastle by club chairman Sir John Hall at a hastily-arranged news conference at St James' Park.

And Dalglish, who has been out of mainstream soccer since June 1995 when he quit as Blackburn's manager a month after taking the title to Ewood Park for the first time in 81 years, said: "I couldn't refuse the job. I'm really looking forward to it."
Dalglish replaced Keegan, who suddenly quit Newcastle last Wednesday after almost five years in charge.

The shortlist for Keegan's replacement quickly came down to two men --- Dalglish and Bobby Robson, but while Robson, a personal friend of Sir John and Sir John's choice -- Dalglish was favoured by the other three decision-making executives who finally won the multi-millionaire architect of the modern Newcastle over.
On Tuesday Sir John paid tribute to Keegan before welcoming Dalglish to the club.
"I would like to place on record my thanks and my board's sincere thanks to Kevin Keegan for five wonderful years.

"To move forward to the new millennium we need a new manager to take us there and I am delighted to welcome Kenny Dalglish. I am certain with his record he will do wonders at this club, a club with great expectations."
Dalglish said he was looking forward to the job.

"I couldn't refuse it, Newcastle is a huge club," he told reporters. "Kevin did a superb job in the five years he was here and any time he wants to come back here and visit the club he will be very welcome. This is not the kind of job that comes along every day because Kevin has left a great foundation for me to build on."

When Keegan took over in February 1992, Newcastle were facing relegation to the old third division for the first time in their history. Dalglish is taking over a club fourth in the premier league, five points behind leaders Liverpool with a game in hand and still in with a very real chance of landing their first title since 1927. They are also in the quarter-finals of the UEFA Cup and still involved in the F.A. Cup.

That is a measure of how far they have come, and with the failure to win the title last season, despite holding a 12-point lead in January, now consigned to the history books of the Keegan era, none of those prizes is out of Newcastle's reach.

Asked whether he could bring the title back to Newcastle this season, Dalglish replied: "If you set targets and do not reach them that can be seen as a failure." Then, smiling broadly he said: "But we've got a much better chance than many other teams."
The one question mark that hangs over Dalglish is that like Keegan, he has quit high pressure jobs because of stress, a reason Keegan gave for leaving Newcastle.
Dalglish left Liverpool in February 1991 citing stress as a cause and his departure from Blackburn after the end of the successful 1995 title campaign was also said to be because of the same reason.

But Dalglish dismissed that on Tuesday saying: "I left Liverpool, which is well-versed, because I was unable to do the job but there were two disasters (Heysel 1985, Hillsborough 1989) in 14 years service. And I left Blackburn because I was trying to protect (then-manager) Ray Harford a little bit, because there were internal problems there -- but they were footballing reasons."

Dalglish will work with many familiar faces at Newcastle. Current assistant manager Terry McDermott is an old Liverpool playing partner, while former Blackburn players Alan Shearer, who moved from Rovers for a world record fee of 15 million pounds ($25 million) last summer, and David Batty, were both members of Dalglish's title-winning squad at Blackburn.

As soon as news of Dalglish's appointment was confirmed, bookmakers Ladbrokes cut their title odds from 5-1 to 9-2 with a spokesman saying: "If anyone can improve Kevin Keegan's team and take Newcastle on to championship glory it is Kenny Dalglish. His track record speaks for itself."

Dalglish, has as both player and manager, won a total of 13 championships in both England and Scotland. In 1977 he followed in Keegan's footsteps as a player at Liverpool and went on to outshine Keegan's considerably successful career there with more titles and Cups than Keegan ever won.
Now he has succeeded Keegan again. A million Geordies are hoping that history is about to repeat itself for their success-starved club.
